seo.title: Quran 4:24 and 15 More Verses on Slaves and Captives, With Tafsir
seo.description: Ibn Kathir and al-Tabari on 16 Quran passages about slaves and 'what your right hands own', from 4:24 and the captives of Awtas to the writ of freedom in 24:33.

page.h1: 16 Qurʾān passages on slaves and “what your right (hands) own”, with Ibn Kathīr and al-Ṭabarī
page.intro: Many Muslims today hold that the Qurʾān set slavery on a path to its end, citing its call to free slaves (90:13) and to write the writ of freedom (24:33). Ibn Kathīr (d. 774 AH, years after the Hijra), author of one of the best-known commentaries on the Qurʾān (tafsīr), which Quran.com offers in English, and al-Ṭabarī (d. 310 AH), whose commentary gathers the readings of the Companions and their students with their chains, read its phrase “what your right (hands) own” as slave-women lawful to their owners without marriage, and captives as lawful after a waiting period. These are the 16 passages, each with what both commentators say it means.

women.question: What does the Qurʾān allow with captive and slave women?
women.dek: Seven passages set “what your right (hands) own” beside wives, beginning with 4:24 and the women captured at Awṭās, where the Prophet sent an army after the Battle of Ḥunayn against the tribe of Hawāzin. Ibn Kathīr and al-Ṭabarī read the phrase in them as slave-women.

parables.question: How do the Qurʾān's parables picture the slave and the master?
parables.dek: Three parables argue from a master and his slave against worshipping others beside God. Both commentators read them as parables.

household.question: What household rules does the Qurʾān give for slaves?
household.dek: Four passages give rules on marrying off slaves, on asking permission to enter, and on the people before whom women need not cover their charms or keep a screen.

freeing.question: What does the Qurʾān say about freeing slaves and treating them well?
freeing.dek: 24:33 commands the writ of freedom, a contract by which a slave buys his freedom (mukātaba), for slaves who seek it, and 4:36 commands good to “what your right (hands) own”. A note lists the other verses Muslims cite on freeing slaves and on captives.

verse-4-24.title: Qurʾān 4:24: Married Women Are Forbidden, “except what your right (hands) own”, and the Captives of Awṭās
verse-4-24.context: Qurʾān 4:24, in Sūrat al-Nisāʾ (Women), follows directly on the list of women a man may not marry (4:23), and its exception bears on whether a woman taken captive was lawful to her captor without marriage.
verse-4-24.hook: In Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī, who fought in twelve campaigns with the Prophet ([Bukhārī 1995](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:1995)), ties 4:24 to the women captured at Awṭās after the Battle of Ḥunayn: married captives became lawful to the Companions “when their 'Idda period came to an end”—where Muslim's gloss uses the general word for a waiting period (ʿidda) and the jurists call a captive's one-cycle wait to make sure she is not pregnant istibrāʾ. Ibn Kathīr reads the exception as captives; al-Ṭabarī adds that the idol-worshipping captives of Awṭās became lawful “when they embraced Islam”.
verse-4-24.takeaway: Muslim 1456a gives the captives of Awṭās as the occasion of 4:24; Ibn Kathīr reads the exception as “those whom you acquire through captivity”, lawful “after making sure they are not pregnant”.

items.work: the English of A. J. Droge, The Qurʾān: A New Annotated Translation (2013), the translation this site uses
items.text: And (also forbidden to you are) married women, except what your right (hands) own. (This is) a written decree of God for you.

items.work: Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 1456a: after the captives were taken at Awṭās
items.text: the Companions of Allah's Messenger … seemed to refrain from having intercourse with captive women because of their husbands being polytheists. Then Allah, Most High, sent down regarding that: "And women already married, except those whom your right hands possess (iv. 24)" (i. e. they were lawful for them when their 'Idda period came to an end)
except those whom you acquire through captivity, for you are allowed to have sexual relations with them after making sure they are not pregnant, as the Ayah was revealed in that regard.

items.work: Tafsīr, on 4:24, his own comment, on married captives from the People of the Book (Jews and Christians)
items.text: those whom we captured from the People of the Two Books who have husbands, for indeed captivity makes them lawful for the one who captured them after the waiting period (istibra')

tafsirQuotes.who: Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī, in Imam Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal's Musnad, a large hadith collection arranged by Companion, as Ibn Kathīr gives it
tafsirQuotes.text: We captured some women from the area of Awtas who were already married, and we disliked having sexual relations with them because they already had husbands. So, we asked the Prophet (peace be upon him) about this matter, and this Ayah was revealed

tafsirQuotes.who: Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī, concluding the same report in Ibn Kathīr, after the verse
tafsirQuotes.text: Consequently, we considered their private parts lawful.

tafsirQuotes.who: Ibn ʿAbbās, recorded by al-Ṭabarī (report no. 7125)
tafsirQuotes.lead: Ibn ʿAbbās, the Prophet's young cousin, for whom the Prophet prayed that God teach him the Book ([Bukhārī 75](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:75)):
tafsirQuotes.text: Every woman who has a husband is forbidden to you, except a female slave you own who has a husband in the land of war; she is lawful to you if you observe the waiting period for her (istibra').

tafsirQuotes.lead: On the two kinds of ownership he reads in “what your right (hands) own” (Ibn Taymiyya, the Ḥanbalī scholar, ranked al-Ṭabarī's commentary the soundest in people's hands):
tafsirQuotes.text: I mean the ownership of the neck (slavery) and the ownership of enjoyment through marriage, because our right hands own all of that. As for the latter, it is ownership of enjoyment, and as for the former, it is ownership of service, enjoyment, and disposal in whatever is permitted to her master from her.

tafsirQuotes.lead: Closing his answer to early authorities who held that a slave-woman's sale ends her marriage, using the story of Barīra, a slave woman who bought her freedom by contract with ʿĀʾishah's help and became ʿĀʾishah's freed slave:
tafsirQuotes.text: Since he gave her the choice, it indicates the continuation of the marriage, and that the meaning of the Ayah refers only to captive women, and Allah knows best.

classical.text:
Ibn Kathīr reads the exception as captives: a married woman taken captive is lawful to her captor “after making sure they are not pregnant”, because the verse came down about Awṭās. Ibn Kathīr records that Ibn Masʿūd and Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, two of the four men the Prophet named to learn the Qurʾān from ([Bukhārī 3808](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:3808)), held with Ibn ʿAbbās that selling a married slave-woman ends her marriage; the majority read the verse as being about captives. Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī (d. 110 AH), the famous preacher and scholar of Basra, is among those he lists for “her sale is her divorce”, and the majority answered with Barīra, to whom the Prophet gave a choice after she was freed.

Al-Ṭabarī reads the verse more broadly: the phrase covers ownership by slavery and by marriage, and selling a married slave-woman “does not mandate separation between her and her husband”. For the Awṭās captives, who were idol-worshippers, he adds a condition: “if they were captives, they became lawful when they embraced Islam by the waiting period (istibra').” That is a waiting period of one menstrual cycle, to make sure she is not pregnant (istibrāʾ). Al-Nawawī, in his commentary on Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, gives the same condition for the Shāfiʿī school and reads the Awṭās report as meaning the captives had become Muslim ([Sharḥ Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, 10/30](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/53/4346/)).

Al-Ṭabarī also records early authorities who read the exception as the four wives taken by contract: the Successors (tābiʿūn), the generation that learned from the Companions and that the Prophet ranked next after his own ([Bukhārī 2652](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:2652)), Abū al-ʿĀliya, ʿUbayda, Ṭāwūs, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr and ʿAṭāʾ, with Ibn ʿAbbās in one of two reports.

verse-4-24.comparison:
Al-Ṭabarī's condition needs the Awṭās captives to have embraced Islam before the Companions went in to them. No report of the event says so, and al-Ṭabarī cites none; he argues from a rule, that “the women of idol worshippers are not lawful through ownership exclusive of Islam” ([al-Ṭabarī on 4:24](/quran/4/24/tafsir/tabari)). For captives from the People of the Book he sets the waiting period alone: “captivity makes them lawful for the one who captured them after the waiting period” (al-Ṭabarī on 4:24). Al-Nawawī gives the rule as that of al-Shāfiʿī, the school's founder, and the scholars who agree with him, calls the same reading of the report necessary, and he too cites no report ([Sharḥ Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, 10/30](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/53/4346/)). The reports of Awṭās name one condition, the end of a waiting period: Muslim's ends on it, and in [Abū Dāwūd 2157](https://sunnah.com/abudawud:2157) the Prophet sets a birth, or one menstrual period; Abū Dāwūd is one of the Sunan collections that rank after Bukhārī and Muslim among the six books, whose reports are graded one by one. Ibn al-Qayyim, in Zād al-Maʿād, his book on the Prophet's practice, makes this point against the condition: no report has the Prophet require these captives' Islam, and he judges it very unlikely that several thousand captives, none of them compelled, all became Muslim ([Zād al-Maʿād 5/120–121](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/127/1034/)).

Some readers today hold that relations with a captive required marriage, citing 4:25, or the early authorities al-Ṭabarī records who read the exception as the four wives taken by contract. Those authorities are Successors, the generation the Prophet ranked next after his own, with Ibn ʿAbbās in one of two reports; their words concern the number of wives. Al-Ṭabarī keeps their reading and adds ownership to it: the phrase covers “the ownership of the neck (slavery) and the ownership of enjoyment through marriage” ([al-Ṭabarī on 4:24](/quran/4/24/tafsir/tabari)). Read of Awṭās, the marriage reading needs a marriage there; the reports name none. Abū Saʿīd's words are “we considered their private parts lawful” (Ibn Kathīr on 4:24), and both commentators read [4:25](/quran/4/25/tafsir/tabari) as a man marrying another's slave-woman with her owner's permission.

The witness is Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī, who was on this campaign: “We captured some women from the area of Awtas”, as Ibn Kathīr gives his words. Ibn Kathīr traces the report to Muslim and to three of the Sunan collections, Abū Dāwūd, al-Tirmidhī and al-Nasāʾī, and al-Dhahabī, author of Siyar Aʿlām al-Nubalāʾ, a biographical dictionary of Muslim scholars, counts 1,170 hadith from him ([IslamWeb, quoting the Siyar](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/fatwa/94125/)).

Either the captives all embraced Islam within the waiting period, which no report of Awṭās records and which the jurists supply from their rule; or the waiting period was the one condition, as the reports and Ibn Kathīr's majority give it, and al-Ṭabarī's condition comes from the rule, not from the event. In neither does a report name a marriage. Abū Saʿīd: “they were lawful for them when their 'Idda period came to an end” ([Muslim 1456a](https://sunnah.com/muslim:1456a)).

verse-23-5-6.title: Qurʾān 23:5–6: Guarding Chastity “except from their wives or what their right (hands) own”
verse-23-5-6.context: Qurʾān 23:5–6 belongs to the opening of Sūrat al-Muʾminūn (The Believers), a list of the qualities of the believers (23:1–11), and says with whom a believer may have relations.
verse-23-5-6.hook: The verse exempts two groups from the duty to guard chastity, “their wives” and “what their right (hands) own”, and the wording returns in 70:29–30. Al-Ṭabarī reads the second group as “their female slaves”; Ibn Kathīr, as slave-women “from the captives”.
verse-23-5-6.takeaway: Al-Ṭabarī reads “what their right (hands) own” in 23:6 as “their female slaves”; Ibn Kathīr as “their right hand possessions from the captives”.

items.text: except from their wives or what their right (hands) own – surely then they are not (to be) blamed,
do not approach anyone except the wives whom Allah has made permissible for them, or their right hand possessions from the captives.

whoever does not guard his private part from his wife and his right hand possession, and guards it from the rest of creation, he is neither rebuked for that, nor condemned, nor is he, by doing that, committing a sin for which he is to be blamed.

tafsirQuotes.text: He means by that: their female slaves.
Allah has approved for them to approach their wives and what their right hands own.

tafsirQuotes.who: Qatāda, as Ibn Kathīr gives the report from al-Ṭabarī
tafsirQuotes.lead: Qatāda, the blind scholar of Basra who narrated from Anas, and whom al-Dhahabī calls a model for commentators and hadith scholars, on a woman who took her male slave, citing this verse. Ibn Kathīr calls the report “a strange, interrupted narration”, a broken chain, with a missing link (munqaṭiʿ):
tafsirQuotes.text: So she was brought to 'Umar bin Al-Khattab. Some of the Companions of the Prophet (peace and blessings of Allah be upon him) said to him: "She interpreted an Ayah from the Book of Allah in a way other than its true meaning." So he banished the slave and shaved his head.

classical.text: Both commentators read the verse as naming two groups. Al-Ṭabarī glosses the first as “wives whom Allah has made permissible for men through marriage” and the second as “their female slaves”, and says “the people of interpretation said similar”; Ibn Kathīr reads the second as slave-women “from the captives”. Ibn Kathīr also records a report, which he calls “a strange, interrupted narration”, in which ʿUmar punished a woman who had applied the verse to her male slave.

verse-23-5-6.comparison:
A reading offered today takes “what their right (hands) own” here as wives, or as women a man has married. It needs the verse's “or” to join two names for one group. Neither commentary reads it so: al-Ṭabarī joins the phrase to “wives” as a second group and glosses it “their female slaves”, and Ibn Kathīr explains what lies beyond as “other than a wife or slave girl” (Ibn Kathīr on 23:6). The best reply is al-Ṭabarī's own reading of 4:24, where the phrase covers “the ownership of enjoyment through marriage” ([al-Ṭabarī on 4:24](/quran/4/24/tafsir/tabari)); there he names two kinds of ownership, and at 23:6 the verse names wives first and he reads the phrase as the slave-women.

Al-Ṭabarī says the people of interpretation agreed, and records Ibn ʿAbbās: “Allah has approved for them to approach their wives and what their right hands own.” The one early dispute Ibn Kathīr records, which he grades “a strange, interrupted narration”, is over a woman applying the verse to her male slave.

Either the phrase names wives a second time, against the “or” and every reading in both commentaries, and then 4:3's “(marry only) one, or what your right (hands) own” offers a wife or a wife; or it names a second group beside wives, as both commentators read it, with the waiting period of 4:24 as the condition they set for captives. The verse: “except from their wives or what their right (hands) own – surely then they are not (to be) blamed,” (23:6).

verse-70-29-30.title: Qurʾān 70:29–30: The Same Exception for “what their right (hands) own” in a Second Sūrah
verse-70-29-30.context: Qurʾān 70:29–30, in Sūrat al-Maʿārij (The Stairways), is part of a description of “the ones who pray” (70:22–35), and repeats in a second sūrah the exception for wives and “what their right (hands) own”.
verse-70-29-30.hook: 70:30 repeats the exception of 23:6 almost word for word, in Sūrat al-Maʿārij. Ibn Kathīr and al-Ṭabarī gloss it as they gloss 23:6: “their female slaves”.
verse-70-29-30.takeaway: 70:30 repeats the exception of 23:6; Ibn Kathīr glosses it “meaning, from their female slaves.”

items.label: Qurʾān 70:30
items.text: except concerning their wives or what their right (hands) own – surely then they are not (to be) blamed,

items.label: Qurʾān 23:6
items.text: except from their wives or what their right (hands) own – surely then they are not (to be) blamed,

tafsirQuotes.text: meaning, from their female slaves.
(Except) that they are not blameworthy in leaving their guarding, (concerning their wives or what their right (hands) own) of their female slaves.

classical.text: Both commentators gloss the phrase as at 23:6: Ibn Kathīr, “meaning, from their female slaves”, and al-Ṭabarī, “of their female slaves”.

verse-70-29-30.comparison: The reading of the phrase as wives meets the same test here as at 23:6: the “or” sets a second group beside wives, and both commentators gloss it as slave-women. In Droge's English the two verses differ by one word, “from” in 23:6 and “concerning” in 70:30: “except concerning their wives or what their right (hands) own – surely then they are not (to be) blamed,” (70:30).

verse-33-50.title: Qurʾān 33:50: What Was Made Lawful to the Prophet, and the 4 Women Ibn Kathīr Says He Owned
verse-33-50.context: Qurʾān 33:50, in Sūrat al-Aḥzāb (The Confederates), is addressed to the Prophet and lists the women made lawful to him.
verse-33-50.hook: 33:50 makes lawful to the Prophet “what your right (hand) owns from what God has given you”, which al-Ṭabarī reads as captives taken in the conquests. Ibn Kathīr names four women: Ṣafiyya, a Jewish woman of Khaybar, taken captive there, and Juwayriyya, daughter of the chief of Banū al-Muṣṭaliq, taken captive in the raid on her tribe, whom the Prophet freed and married; and Rayḥāna, a woman taken captive from Banū Qurayẓa, the Jewish tribe of Medina, and Māriya the Copt, mother of the Prophet's infant son Ibrāhīm, “among the concubines”.
verse-33-50.takeaway: Ibn Kathīr on 33:50: “He owned Safiyyah and Juwayriyah, then freed them and married them”; he counts Rayḥāna and Māriya “among the concubines”.

items.text: Prophet! Surely We have made lawful for you your wives to whom you have granted their marriage gifts, and what your right (hand) owns from what God has given you,

And We have made lawful for you your female slaves whom you have taken as captives, and thus owned them through captivity, and who have become yours due to the conquests God bestowed upon you as spoils of war.

He also permitted you to take concubines from what you have taken from the war booty. He owned Safiyyah and Juwayriyah, then freed them and married them. He also owned Rayhanah bint Sham'un An-Nadariyyah, and Mariyah Al-Qibtiyyah, the mother of his son Ibrahim, peace be upon him; and they were among the concubines, may Allah be pleased with them.

tafsirQuotes.text: The same was the case with Juwayriyah bint Al-Harith Al-Mustaliqiyyah, for whom he paid off her contract of manumission to Thabit bin Qays bin Shammas and married her.

tafsirQuotes.who: Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, early commentators and al-Ṭabarī, as Ibn Kathīr gives them
tafsirQuotes.lead: Ubayy ibn Kaʿb was one of the four men the Prophet named to learn the Qurʾān from ([Bukhārī 3808](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:3808)), whom ʿUmar called our best reciter ([Bukhārī 4481](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:4481)). On “We know what We have made obligatory for them concerning their wives and what their right (hands) own”:
tafsirQuotes.text: Regarding limiting them to four free women and whatever concubines they wish

classical.text: Al-Ṭabarī reads “what your right (hand) owns from what God has given you” as captives who became the Prophet's “due to the conquests God bestowed upon you as spoils of war”. Ibn Kathīr states that the Prophet freed and married Ṣafiyya and Juwayriyya, paying off the contract by which Juwayriyya was buying her freedom, and counts Rayḥāna and Māriya “among the concubines”. For the believers, he gives the reading of Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, Mujāhid, al-Ḥasan, Qatāda and al-Ṭabarī: “limiting them to four free women and whatever concubines they wish”.

verse-33-50.comparison:
The answer that the Prophet's captives became freed, honoured wives needs every woman under this phrase to have been freed and married. Ibn Kathīr, who records the freeing, says it of two: “He owned Safiyyah and Juwayriyah, then freed them and married them.” Of Rayḥāna and Māriya he says “they were among the concubines” ([Ibn Kathīr on 33:50](/quran/33/50/tafsir/ibn_kathir)).

For Rayḥāna the biographers differ. Ibn Saʿd (d. 230 AH) records from al-Wāqidī (d. 207 AH) that the Prophet freed her and married her ([Ṭabaqāt 8/129](https://ablibrary.net/book_content/b/17778/102)), though the hadith critics including al-Bukhārī, Muslim, and Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal left al-Wāqidī's narrations ([al-Mizzī, Tahdhīb al-Kamāl](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/1001/6686/)). Ibn Isḥāq (d. 150 AH), in the edition of Ibn Hishām, says the Prophet offered to marry her and veil her, she asked to stay in his ownership as lighter for both of them, and she was in his ownership when he died ([Sīrat Ibn Hishām](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/200/17323/)). For Māriya, mother of Ibrāhīm, a report in Ibn Mājah says “Her son set her free” ([Ibn Mājah 2516](https://sunnah.com/ibnmajah:2516)); it is graded weak (ḍaʿīf).

Either Rayḥāna was freed and married, as al-Wāqidī has it, against Ibn Isḥāq's report and Ibn Kathīr's list; or she stayed in his ownership, as they say. In both, Māriya is counted among the concubines, and the verse's phrase is not limited to women freed and married. On the verse's later clause for the believers, “We know what We have made obligatory for them concerning their wives and what their right (hands) own”, Ibn Kathīr gives the reading of Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, early commentators and al-Ṭabarī: “limiting them to four free women and whatever concubines they wish” ([Ibn Kathīr on 33:50](/quran/33/50/tafsir/ibn_kathir)).

verse-4-3.title: Qurʾān 4:3: Up to Four Wives, or “(marry only) one, or what your right (hands) own”
verse-4-3.context: Qurʾān 4:3, in a passage on the care of orphans near the opening of Sūrat al-Nisāʾ (Women) (4:2–6), is the verse that permits up to four wives, and its second option bears on whether a slave-woman was taken by marriage or by ownership.
verse-4-3.hook: 4:3 permits up to four wives and, to the man who fears he will not be fair, “(marry only) one, or what your right (hands) own”. Al-Ṭabarī reads the second option as concubines, to whom a man is “not obligated … with the rights like those you are obligated to free women”.
verse-4-3.takeaway: Both commentators read the second option of 4:3 as the lighter duty; al-Ṭabarī: a man is “not obligated to them with the rights like those you are obligated to free women”, “because they are your property and your wealth”.

items.text: But if you fear that you will not be fair, (marry only) one, or what your right (hands) own. That (will make it) more likely that you will not be biased.

So whoever fears that, let him limit himself to one wife, or to female slave concubines, for it is not obligatory to divide time among them, rather it is recommended. So if one does so, that is good, and if not, there is no harm.

then do not marry her, but take concubines from the slaves. For it is more likely that you will not act unjustly toward them, because they are your property and your wealth, and you are not obligated to them with the rights like those you are obligated to free women.

tafsirQuotes.lead: Setting aside the reading of “That (will make it) more likely that you will not be biased” as “more likely that your dependents do not become numerous”, before he gives the majority view, “that you do not do injustice”:
tafsirQuotes.text: However, this interpretation here is questionable; because just as a large number of dependents is feared from a multitude of free wives, it is also feared from a multitude of concubines.

tafsirQuotes.lead: On “to seek (to obtain) by means of your wealth”:
tafsirQuotes.text: you are allowed to use your money to obtain up to four wives or as many female slaves as you wish, through legal means

classical.text: Al-Ṭabarī reads the second option as taking concubines, says the commentators (ahl al-taʾwīl, his “people of interpretation”) held the same, and gives the reason “because they are your property and your wealth”. Ibn Kathīr calls dividing time among slave-women recommended rather than obligatory, and on 4:24 allows “as many female slaves as you wish”. On the verse's closing reason he follows the majority, “that you do not do injustice”, and sets aside the reading “more likely that your dependents do not become numerous”, since dependents can come from “a multitude of concubines” as well as from many wives.

verse-4-3.comparison:
A reading offered today takes the second option as marriage to a slave-woman, with “marry” carried over from the first. It needs a commentator or report that reads it so; neither commentary gives one. Al-Ṭabarī reads it the other way: to the man who fears injustice “regarding the matter of one”, the verse says “then do not marry her, but take concubines from the slaves” (al-Ṭabarī on 4:3), and he says the people of interpretation held the same; and al-Suddī (d. 127 AH), a commentator of Kūfa who narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās and from Anas ibn Mālik, who served the Prophet for ten years ([Bukhārī 6038](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:6038)), glosses the phrase as concubines, as al-Ṭabarī records. The marriage of a slave-woman has its own verse, [4:25](/quran/4/25/tafsir/tabari), for the man who “cannot wait to marry believing, free women”.

Both commentators explain the verse's reason, “That (will make it) more likely that you will not be biased”, by the lighter duty: Ibn Kathīr says dividing time among slave-women “is not obligatory” (Ibn Kathīr on 4:3).

Either the second option is marriage to a slave-woman, a reading neither commentary records; or it is ownership, as the people of interpretation read it, with the lighter duty as the reason the verse gives. Al-Ṭabarī: “because they are your property and your wealth, and you are not obligated to them with the rights like those you are obligated to free women.” ([al-Ṭabarī on 4:3](/quran/4/3/tafsir/tabari))

verse-33-52.title: Qurʾān 33:52: No More Wives for the Prophet, “except for what your right (hand) owns”
verse-33-52.context: Qurʾān 33:52, in Sūrat al-Aḥzāb, comes two verses after 33:50, in the same passage addressed to the Prophet about his wives.
verse-33-52.hook: 33:52 forbids the Prophet further wives, “except for what your right (hand) owns”. Ibn Kathīr says the verse rewarded his wives and was later lifted, and that the exception covered “female slaves and concubines, regarding whom there was no restriction”.
verse-33-52.takeaway: Ibn Kathīr on 33:52: the Prophet was restricted to his wives “with the exception of female slaves and concubines, regarding whom there was no restriction.”

showcase.note: Ibn Kathīr adds that the restriction was later lifted: “Then Allah lifted the restriction on him in that regard and abrogated the ruling of this Ayah, permitting him to marry, but he did not marry any other women after that”.

items.text: Beyond (that) women are not permitted to you, nor (is it permitted to you) to take (other) wives in exchange for them
Allah restricted him to them, and forbade him to marry anyone else or to exchange them for other wives
except for what your right (hand) owns
with the exception of female slaves and concubines, regarding whom there was no restriction.
you have the right to own slave girls from whichever of the races of people you wish.

tafsirQuotes.who: Ibn Kathīr (d. 774 AH), citing Ibn ʿAbbās, early commentators and al-Ṭabarī
tafsirQuotes.text: this Ayah was revealed as a reward to the wives of the Prophet and indicating Allah's pleasure with them for their excellent conduct in choosing Allah, His Messenger, and the Home of the Hereafter

Women are not permitted to you after those whom I have permitted to you except what your right hand owns of slave girls, for you have the right to own slave girls from whichever of the races of people you wish.

classical.text: Ibn Kathīr, citing Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, Qatāda, Ibn Zayd and al-Ṭabarī, says the verse rewarded the Prophet's wives for choosing him, and that the restriction was later lifted, citing ʿĀʾisha: “The Messenger of Allah did not die until Allah made women permissible for him.” He adds “but he did not marry any other women after that”. Al-Ṭabarī reads the restriction as “after those whom I have permitted to you” in 33:50, and records the same report from ʿĀʾisha.

verse-33-52.comparison: Ibn Kathīr's account needs a later permission that lifted the restriction; he gives one, ʿĀʾisha's report, which al-Ṭabarī also records. The readings differ over wives, restricted to the end or released. On slaves they agree: the exception stood in the verse from the start, and Ibn Kathīr explains it “with the exception of female slaves and concubines, regarding whom there was no restriction.” The verse: “nor (is it permitted to you) to take (other) wives in exchange for them, even though their beauty pleases you, except for what your right (hand) owns.” (33:52)

verse-4-25.title: Qurʾān 4:25: Marrying a Believing Slave-Woman, and Half the Punishment of Free Women
verse-4-25.context: Qurʾān 4:25, in Sūrat al-Nisāʾ, comes right after 4:24 and addresses the man who cannot marry a free believing woman; readers today cite it on whether relations with a slave-woman required marriage.
verse-4-25.hook: 4:25 permits the man who cannot marry a free believing woman to marry a believing slave-woman “with the permission of their families”. Ibn Kathīr reads this as her owner's permission and explains the counsel to be patient by her children, who would be slaves.
verse-4-25.takeaway: 4:25 permits marrying a believing slave-woman “with the permission of their families”; Ibn Kathīr reads this as her owner's permission and says the children “will become slaves to the girl’s master”.

items.text: (let them take) believing young women from what your right (hands) own. God knows your belief, (for) you are all alike. Marry them with the permission of their families, and give them their rightful marriage gifts
indicating that the owner is responsible for the slave girl, and consequently, she cannot marry without his permission.

And that half which God appointed as punishment for whoever commits immorality among the slave women if they are protected (uhsinna) is: fifty lashes, and banishment for six months, and that is half a year.

tafsirQuotes.text: if he marries her, his offspring will become slaves to the girl’s master - unless the husband is an Arab, then his children from her will not be slaves, according to an old opinion of Ash-Shafi'i.

tafsirQuotes.lead: On “Yet to be patient (would be) better for you”:
tafsirQuotes.text: that you be patient and not marry a slave girl resulting in your children being owned slaves, it is better for you.

tafsirQuotes.who: al-Shāfiʿī, as Ibn Kathīr gives him
tafsirQuotes.text: The Muslims did not differ that there is no stoning upon an owned slave for fornication.

tafsirQuotes.lead: On whether a slave-woman is also exiled:
tafsirQuotes.text: There are three opinions on this: The first is that she is exiled. The second is that she is not exiled at all, and this is the view of 'Ali and the jurists of Al-Madinah. The third is that she is exiled for half a year, which is half the exile of a free woman.

classical.text: Ibn Kathīr reads “with the permission of their families” as the owner's permission, and records that the majority allowed such a marriage on two conditions, no means to marry a free woman and fear of sin, which Abū Ḥanīfa, founder of the Ḥanafī school, one of the four Sunni schools of law, and his companions did not require. He gives al-Shāfiʿī's statement that there is no stoning for a slave and records three opinions on exile. Al-Ṭabarī reads the same words as “with the permission of their masters”, and sets the half at “fifty lashes, and banishment for six months”.

verse-4-25.comparison:
Some readers today take this verse to show that relations with any slave-woman required marriage. That reading needs the verse to address the slave-woman's owner. Both commentators read it as a man marrying another's slave: al-Ṭabarī reads “with the permission of their families” as “with the permission of their masters” (al-Ṭabarī on 4:25), and Ibn Kathīr says “she cannot marry without his permission”.

Ibn Kathīr, and al-Suddī as al-Ṭabarī records him, explain the closing counsel by the children, who in Ibn Kathīr's words “will become slaves to the girl’s master” (Ibn Kathīr on 4:25); the verse is addressed to “Whoever among you cannot wait to marry believing, free women”.

Either the verse governs a man's own slave-women: he would ask his own permission to marry them, and the reason given for the counsel, children who become slaves to her master, would make them slaves to their own father; or it governs marrying another man's slave-woman, as both commentators read it, and leaves the owner to 4:24, 23:6 and 4:3. Al-Suddī on the counsel, as al-Ṭabarī records him (report no. 9123): “that you be patient and not marry a slave girl resulting in your children being owned slaves, it is better for you.” ([al-Ṭabarī on 4:25](/quran/4/25/tafsir/tabari))

verse-16-75.title: Qurʾān 16:75: The Parable of “a slave (who is) owned – he has no power over anything”
verse-16-75.context: Qurʾān 16:75, in Sūrat al-Naḥl (The Bee), is the first of two parables (16:75–76) that follow a verse on serving what “has no power to provide anything” (16:73), and its argument rests on what its hearers knew of an owned slave.
verse-16-75.hook: 16:75 sets “a slave (who is) owned – he has no power over anything” beside a man who spends from his provision, and asks “Are they equal?” Ibn Kathīr and al-Ṭabarī record two readings of the parable: the unbeliever and the believer, or the idol and God.
verse-16-75.takeaway: Ibn Kathīr and al-Ṭabarī read 16:75 as a parable of the unbeliever and the believer; al-Ṭabarī pictures “the slave who owns nothing and has no power over anything”.

showcase.note: The verse puts its own question: “Are they equal?” (16:75)

items.text: a slave (who is) owned – he has no power over anything
like the owned slave, who has no power over anything to contribute from it.
(another) whom We have provided with a good provision from Us, and he contributes from it in secret and in public
like the free man whom God has given wealth, so he contributes from it in secret and in public.

tafsirQuotes.who: Ibn ʿAbbās, as Ibn Kathīr gives him (also Qatāda, preferred by al-Ṭabarī)
tafsirQuotes.text: This is a parable that Allah struck for the disbeliever and the believer.

tafsirQuotes.who: Mujāhid, as Ibn Kathīr gives him
tafsirQuotes.lead: Mujāhid, who went through the Qurʾān with Ibn ʿAbbās three times, stopping at every verse to ask about it:
tafsirQuotes.text: It is a parable struck for the idol and for the True God, Exalted be He. So are they equal?
Is the slave who owns nothing and has no power over anything equal to this free man whom God has provided with a good provision so that he contributes as He described?

classical.text: Ibn Kathīr gives two readings: Ibn ʿAbbās and Qatāda, followed by al-Ṭabarī, saw the unbeliever and the believer; Mujāhid saw the idol and God. Both commentators explain the verse as a parable.

verse-16-75.comparison: Both commentators read the verse as a parable and draw no ruling from it; the readings they record differ on whom it pictures, the unbeliever and the believer, or the idol and God. The answer that the slaves of these texts were servants needs the parable's first figure to be something other than the slave its hearers owned. Neither commentator reads it so: al-Ṭabarī sets “the owned slave” against “the free man whom God has given wealth” ([al-Ṭabarī on 16:75](/quran/16/75/tafsir/tabari)). The parable works in either reading because its hearers agree that the owned slave “has no power over anything”. The verse: “Are they equal? Praise (be) to God! No! But most of them do not know (it).” (16:75)

crossLinks.label: The answer: were they servants or slaves? →

verse-16-71.title: Qurʾān 16:71: The Favoured Do Not Share Their Provision With “what their right (hands) own”
verse-16-71.context: Qurʾān 16:71, in Sūrat al-Naḥl (The Bee), comes four verses before the parable of 16:75.
verse-16-71.hook: 16:71 says the favoured do not give over their provision to “what their right (hands) own”. Both commentators, citing Ibn ʿAbbās and early authorities, read it as an argument against associating partners with God.
verse-16-71.takeaway: Ibn ʿAbbās, as Ibn Kathīr records, read 16:71 as an argument against idolatry: “They would never share their wealth and women with their slaves”, so they should not associate God's slaves with Him.

items.text: those who have been favored do not give over their provision to what their right (hands) own, so (that) they are (all) equal in that respect. Is it the blessing of God they deny?

items.work: al-ʿAwfī's report, in Ibn Kathīr on 16:71
items.text: They would never share their wealth and women with their slaves, so how could they associate My slaves with Me in My authority?
Would any of you share his wife and his bed with his slave, such that you equalize Allah's creation and slaves with Allah?
they do not make their owned slaves partners in what He provided for them of wealth and spouses.

tafsirQuotes.text: So they are not content that they and their owned slaves be equal in what I have provided them, yet they have made My slaves My partners in My dominion and My sovereignty. And this is a parable that God, whose mention is exalted, struck for those who associate partners with God.

tafsirQuotes.who: Mujāhid, as Ibn Kathīr gives him
tafsirQuotes.text: This is a parable for the false deities.

classical.text: Both commentators read the verse as an argument against associating partners with God, drawn from what its hearers would not accept for their own slaves.

verse-16-71.comparison: The argument against idolatry in 16:71 starts from the hearers' own households: “those who have been favored do not give over their provision to what their right (hands) own” (16:71). Because the parable works when every hearer takes it as self-evident that a master never shares his wealth on equal terms with his owned slaves, the verse relies on the legal hierarchy between master and slave as an unquestioned baseline of social life.

verse-30-28.title: Qurʾān 30:28: A Parable From “what your right (hands) own”, in 2 Early Readings
verse-30-28.context: Qurʾān 30:28, in Sūrat al-Rūm (The Byzantines), is a parable addressed to those who associate partners with God.
verse-30-28.hook: 30:28 asks whether masters share their provision with “what your right (hands) own”, “fearing them as you fear each other”. Al-Ṭabarī records two readings of that fear: Ibn ʿAbbās's, that slaves would inherit, and that of Abū Mijlaz, a Successor of Basra whom the critics graded reliable, that they would divide the wealth. He prefers the Successor's reading to the Companion's, as closer to the wording.
verse-30-28.takeaway: Al-Ṭabarī prefers Abū Mijlaz's reading of 30:28 to Ibn ʿAbbās's: “you do not fear that your owned slave will divide your wealth with you, and he has no right to that.”

items.text: Among what your right (hands) own, do you have associates in what We have provided you with, so that you are (all) equal in that respect – (you) fearing them as you fear each other?
you fear that they will inherit from you as you inherit from each other.
Indeed, you do not fear that your owned slave will divide your wealth with you, and he has no right to that. Similarly, Allah has no partner.
And the more correct of the two statements in the interpretation of this is the second statement; because it is the most similar of the two to what the apparent wording of the speech indicates.

tafsirQuotes.text: Do you have among your owned slaves any associates in the wealth that We have provided you with, so that you and they are equal in it? He says: If you do not accept this for yourselves, how then can you accept that your gods which you worship are partners with Me in your worship of Me, when both you and they are My slaves and My owned possessions, and I am the Owner of all of you?
none of you would like to have his servant as a partner in his wealth, each of them having an equal share.

classical.text: Al-Ṭabarī prefers Abū Mijlaz's reading (fear of dividing the wealth) over Ibn ʿAbbās's (fear of inheritance), because “the mention of partnership does not indicate a fear of inheritance”. Ibn Kathīr gives Abū Mijlaz's reading.

verse-30-28.comparison: Both early readings start from the question the verse puts to slave-owners: “do you have associates in what We have provided you with, so that you are (all) equal in that respect – (you) fearing them as you fear each other?” (30:28). Whether that fear means a slave inheriting (Ibn ʿAbbās) or dividing the owner's property as a co-owner (Abū Mijlaz and al-Ṭabarī), the Qurʾān treats the legal gulf between a free master and his owned slave as the common-sense premise from which it argues that created beings cannot be partners with God.

verse-24-32.title: Qurʾān 24:32: Marrying Off the Unmarried and “the righteous among your male slaves and your female slaves”
verse-24-32.context: Qurʾān 24:32, in Sūrat al-Nūr (The Light), opens a pair of verses on marriage and on slaves (24:32–33), and addresses owners as the ones who marry their slaves off.
verse-24-32.hook: 24:32 commands the believers to marry off the unmarried and “the righteous among your male slaves and your female slaves”. Ibn ʿAbbās, in both commentaries, says Allah commanded the free and the slaves to marry; Ibn Kathīr records a group that held marriage obligatory on anyone able.
verse-24-32.takeaway: The command in 24:32 is addressed to the believers; Ibn ʿAbbās, as al-Ṭabarī records, says Allah “commanded them to marry off their free men and their slaves”.

items.text: Marry off the unmarried among you, and (also) the righteous among your male slaves and your female slaves. If they are poor, God will enrich them from His favor.

items.work: ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥa's report, in Ibn Kathīr on 24:32
items.text: Allah encouraged them to marry, and commanded the free and the slaves to do so, and promised them wealth for it

If these whom you marry off from among the unmarried of your men and your women, and your male slaves and your female slaves, are people of need and poverty, then Allah will enrich them from His favor, so do not let their poverty prevent you from marrying them off.

tafsirQuotes.who: Ibn ʿAbbās (ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥa's report), recorded by al-Ṭabarī
tafsirQuotes.text: Allah, the Exalted, commanded marriage, and encouraged them towards it, and commanded them to marry off their free men and their slaves, and promised them enrichment in that
This is a command to marry. A group of scholars went to the view that it is obligatory upon anyone who is capable of it.
So marry off your female slaves, for Allah is embracing, He expands (His provision) upon them from His favor, if they are poor.

classical.text: Ibn Kathīr calls the verse “a command to marry” and records that “A group of scholars went to the view that it is obligatory upon anyone who is capable of it.” On 4:25 he adds that a slave-woman “cannot marry without his permission”.

verse-24-32.comparison: In 24:32 the verse speaks to free believers as the ones who arrange marriages for others—the unmarried among them and “the righteous among your male slaves and your female slaves” (24:32). While encouraging owners not to let poverty stop them from marrying off trustworthy slaves, the command presupposes what Ibn Kathīr states on 4:25: a slave does not marry without the owner's permission.

verse-24-58.title: Qurʾān 24:58: Slaves and Children Ask Permission at 3 Times of the Day
verse-24-58.context: Qurʾān 24:58, in Sūrat al-Nūr, gives a rule for entering rooms within the household, and puts slaves under the same rule as children.
verse-24-58.hook: 24:58 has slaves and children ask permission to enter at three times of the day, “the three (times) of nakedness for you”. Ibn Kathīr explains their freedom at other times by their service in the house; al-Ṭabarī holds that the rule covers male and female slaves.
verse-24-58.takeaway: 24:58 sets three times when slaves and children ask permission; Ibn Kathīr explains the freedom at other times: “they are those who go around in the house, i.e., to serve you”.

items.text: “before the dawn prayer, and when you lay down your clothes at the noon hour, and after the evening prayer – the three (times) of nakedness for you.”

Ibn Kathīr: “They have been given permission to enter suddenly, because they are those who go around in the house, i.e., to serve you etc., and as such they may be forgiven for things that others will not be forgiven.”

Al-Ṭabarī: “What is meant by it is males and females; because Allah generalized in His saying: {those whom your right (hands) own}, (meaning) all those possessed by our right hands, and He did not specify a male or a female among them.”

tafsirQuotes.who: Ibn ʿAbbās, in a report Ibn Kathīr calls “authentic to Ibn 'Abbas” (also in Abū Dāwūd)
tafsirQuotes.text: The people did not have curtains on their doors, nor canopies in their houses, so a man's servant, child, or orphan under his care might surprise him while he was with his wife. Thus, Allah commanded them to seek permission during those times of privacy which Allah named.

tafsirQuotes.lead: Ibn ʿUmar, son of the caliph ʿUmar; al-Dhahabī counts 2,630 hadith from him, repeats included ([Siyar 3/238](https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/60/328/)):
tafsirQuotes.text: It applies to males excluding females.

classical.text: Ibn Kathīr gives the reason for the freedom at other times: slaves “go around in the house, i.e., to serve you”. Al-Ṭabarī records a view that the verse meant male slaves (Ibn ʿUmar: “It applies to males excluding females.”) and prefers the view that it covers “males and females”.

verse-24-58.comparison: The verse puts adult slaves and pre-pubescent children under one household privacy rule: “those whom your right (hands) own, and those of you who have not reached the (age of) puberty” ask permission at the three hours of undress (24:58), whereas once a free child reaches puberty he must ask permission at all times (24:59). As both commentators note, the rule regulates a household in which owned slaves move in and out of the family's private rooms throughout the day to serve.

verse-24-31.title: Qurʾān 24:31: Women May Show Their Charms to “what their right (hands) own”, in 2 Readings
verse-24-31.context: Qurʾān 24:31, in Sūrat al-Nūr, lists the people before whom believing women may show their charms.
verse-24-31.hook: 24:31 lists “what their right (hands) own” among those before whom believing women may show their charms. Ibn Kathīr records two readings: a woman's slave-women, the view of two early authorities, or her slaves of both sexes, the view of the majority, who cite a report about Fāṭima.
verse-24-31.takeaway: Ibn Kathīr records 2 readings of “what their right (hands) own” in 24:31: a woman's slave-woman, a polytheist included (Ibn Jurayj); and the majority's, “her slaves, both men and women”.

items.text: or their sisters’ sons, or their women, or what their right (hands) own, or such men as attend (them who) have no (sexual) desire

items.who: Ibn Jurayj (d. 150 AH), the first to set down knowledge in writing at Mecca
items.work: in Ibn Kathīr on 24:31; also the view of Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib, the leading scholar of Medina in the generation after the Companions
items.text: This means from among the women of the polytheists. It is permissible for a Muslim woman to reveal her adornment to her even if she is a polytheist, because she is her slave-girl.

items.work: as Ibn Kathīr records them, on 24:31
items.text: Rather, it is permissible for her to reveal it to her slaves, both men and women.

tafsirQuotes.who: The Prophet to Fāṭima, in a report Ibn Kathīr cites from Abū Dāwūd (Abū Dāwūd 4106)
tafsirQuotes.lead: The majority's evidence, given by Ibn Kathīr: the Prophet had brought Fāṭima a slave as a gift, and her garment could not cover both her head and her feet. Al-Albānī, the modern hadith scholar whose gradings Sunnah.com prints beside reports outside Bukhārī and Muslim, graded it authentic (ṣaḥīḥ).
tafsirQuotes.text: There is no harm upon you; it is only your father and your boy (slave).
Some of them said: Or their owned slaves (Mamalik), for there is no harm upon her to show them of her charm what she shows to these.

classical.text: Ibn Kathīr records two readings: Ibn Jurayj and Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib took the phrase to mean a woman's slave-woman, including a polytheist; the majority held “it is permissible for her to reveal it to her slaves, both men and women”, citing the report of Fāṭima and the slave the Prophet gave her.

verse-24-31.comparison:
The majority's reading, slaves of both sexes, needs the slave in the Fāṭima report to be one before whom she uncovered as before a man. Ibn Kathīr gives that report as their evidence: “There is no harm upon you; it is only your father and your boy (slave).” Abū Dāwūd records it, and al-Albānī graded it authentic. Ibn Kathīr's next lines, from Ibn ʿAsākir (d. 571 AH), author of the History of Damascus, name the slave and say Fāṭima “raised him and then freed him”, which places him as a child when he was given; the verse lists children apart, “children (who are) not (yet) aware of women’s nakedness”.

Either the phrase covers adult male slaves, as the majority read from this report; or the report's slave was a boy, and the phrase means slave-women, as Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib and Ibn Jurayj read it. In the verse it stands between “their women” and the men who “have no (sexual) desire” (24:31).

verse-33-55.title: Qurʾān 33:55: The Prophet's Wives Need No Screen Before “what their right (hands) own”
verse-33-55.context: Qurʾān 33:55, in Sūrat al-Aḥzāb, comes two verses after the command to ask the Prophet's wives for things “from behind a veil” (33:53).
verse-33-55.hook: 33:55 lifts the screen for the Prophet's wives before close kin, their women and “what their right (hands) own”. Ibn Kathīr reads the last as “their slaves, male and female”; Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib, as he records, as female slaves alone.
verse-33-55.takeaway: Ibn Kathīr reads “what their right (hands) own” in 33:55 as “their slaves, male and female”; Ibn Zayd, recorded by al-Ṭabarī, says the Prophet's wives “did not observe Hijab in front of the owned slaves (Mamalik).”

items.text: (There is) no blame on them concerning their fathers, or their sons, or their brothers, or their brothers’ sons, or their sisters’ sons, or their women, or what their right (hands) own.
means their slaves, male and female, as was pointed out previously, along with the Hadith concerning it.
This means female slaves only.

items.who: Ibn Zayd, a Medinan commentator of the second century AH whom the hadith critics graded weak
items.text: And the wives of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, did not observe Hijab in front of the owned slaves (Mamalik).

tafsirQuotes.text: That means the lifting of blame from them concerning these Muslims, that they do not need to observe Hijab in front of them.
And His saying {or what their right (hands) own}, from the men and the women; and others said: From the women.

classical.text: Al-Ṭabarī prefers the reading that the verse lifts the duty of the screen before those it lists, because it follows the verse of the curtain. On the last item, Ibn Kathīr and al-Ṭabarī record two views: slaves male and female, or female slaves alone (Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib).

verse-33-55.comparison: Al-Ṭabarī's preferred reading needs the verse to follow on the verse of the screen (33:53), which it does. On the last item the two views stand side by side, slaves male and female, or female slaves (Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib); Ibn Zayd, recorded by al-Ṭabarī, describes the practice: the Prophet's wives “did not observe Hijab in front of the owned slaves (Mamalik).” The verse sets the phrase at the end of the same list as fathers, sons and brothers: “or their women, or what their right (hands) own.” (33:55)

verse-24-33.title: Qurʾān 24:33: The Writ of Freedom (Mukātaba), and “do not force your young women into prostitution”
verse-24-33.context: Qurʾān 24:33, in Sūrat al-Nūr, follows the command to marry off free people and slaves (24:32).
verse-24-33.hook: 24:33 tells masters to write the writ of freedom, the contract by which a slave buys his freedom, for slaves who seek it, “if you know any good in them”, and forbids forcing slave-girls into prostitution. Mālik, and al-Shāfiʿī in his later view, founders of two of the four Sunni schools of law, took the command as a recommendation; al-Shāfiʿī's earlier view and al-Ṭabarī held it a duty, and so did ʿUmar, who told Anas ibn Mālik, who served the Prophet for ten years ([Bukhārī 6038](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:6038)), to write his slave's contract.
verse-24-33.takeaway: 24:33 tells masters to write a contract of freedom for slaves who seek it; Ibn Kathīr reports that many scholars read this as “recommendation”, and al-Ṭabarī holds it “obligatory” when the slave asks.

items.text: Those who seek the writ, among what your right (hands) own, write (it) for them, if you know any good in them, and give them some of the wealth of God which He has given you. And do not force your young women into prostitution, if they wish (to live in) chastity,
Many of the scholars are of the view that this command is a command of guidance and recommendation, not a command of obligation and requirement.
It is obligatory upon the master of the slave to write a contract of emancipation for him if he knows there is good in him, and the slave asks him for the contract of emancipation.

items.work: in Ibn Kathīr on 24:33, on the occasion; one of the 1,400 at Ḥudaybiya whom the Prophet called the best people on earth (Bukhārī 4154)
items.text: This was revealed about a slave-girl belonging to 'Abdullah bin Ubayy bin Salul whose name was Musaykah. He used to force her to commit immoral actions - and there was nothing wrong with her - but she refused.

tafsirQuotes.text: This is a command from Allah to slave-owners: if their servants ask them for a contract of emancipation, they should write it for them, provided that the servant has a skill and means of earning so that he can pay his master the money that he agreed upon paying.

tafsirQuotes.lead: On the practice of the pre-Islamic age (Jāhiliyya), sending slave-girls into unlawful intercourse (zinā) for a fee:
tafsirQuotes.text: Among the people of the Jahiliyyah, if one of them had a slave-girl, he would send her out to commit Zina, and would set a tax upon her, which he would take from her every time. When Islam came, Allah forbade the Muslims from doing that.

tafsirQuotes.lead: On “give them some of the wealth of God which He has given you”, his preferred reading:
tafsirQuotes.text: He meant by it giving them their share from the obligatory charity.
the burden of sin for what occurred of that is upon them (the masters) exclusive of them (the slaves).

classical.text: Ibn Kathīr reports that many scholars took the command to write the contract as “a command of guidance and recommendation”, among them Mālik, Sufyān al-Thawrī, whom the early critics called the commander of the faithful in hadith, Abū Ḥanīfa and al-Shāfiʿī in his later view, and that others, among them al-Ḍaḥḥāk, an early commentator whom al-Dhahabī calls honest though not precise in hadith, and al-Shāfiʿī in his earlier view, held it obligatory. Al-Ṭabarī holds it obligatory when the slave asks and the master “knows there is good in him”, because a command of Allah binds “unless there is evidence from the Book or Sunnah that it is a recommendation”, and reads “the wealth of God” as the slave's share of the obligatory alms (zakāt), which the Qurʾān lets be spent on freeing slaves ([9:60](/quran/9/60/tafsir/tabari)). Both give the occasion of the second command as a slave-girl of ʿAbdallāh ibn Ubayy, the leader of the hypocrites of Medina ([Bukhārī 1269](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:1269)), and al-Ṭabarī places the sin on the masters.

verse-24-33.comparison:
The reading as a recommendation needs the command “write (it) for them” to be a permission. It cites no report on the writ. Mālik says “I have not heard any of the Imams forcing anyone to write a contract of emancipation for his slave” (Ibn Kathīr on 24:33); people of knowledge he heard compared it to 5:2 and 62:10, commands that follow a ban; and al-Shāfiʿī's later view rests on the rule that a Muslim's wealth needs his consent. No verse before 24:33 bans the writ.

The reading as an obligation cites the act of ʿUmar, the second caliph: when Anas delayed the writ his slave Sīrīn asked for, ʿUmar told him “You should certainly write him a contract of emancipation.” Ibn Kathīr calls the chain authentic, and al-Bukhārī gives, without a connected chain, a version in which ʿUmar struck Anas with the whip.

Either the command bound the master, as ʿUmar applied it and al-Ṭabarī held; or it left the writ to his will, as Mālik and the schools that follow the recommendation held. On both readings the slave pays for his freedom; Ibn Kathīr: “so that he can pay his master the money that he agreed upon paying.” The verse: “Those who seek the writ, among what your right (hands) own, write (it) for them, if you know any good in them” (24:33).

verse-4-36.title: Qurʾān 4:36: “(do) good to” Parents, Orphans, Neighbours… “and what your right (hands) own”
verse-4-36.context: Qurʾān 4:36, in Sūrat al-Nisāʾ, lists those to whom believers are to do good, after the command to serve God.
verse-4-36.hook: 4:36 ends its list of those owed good treatment, from parents and orphans to neighbours and travellers, with “what your right (hands) own”. Ibn Kathīr calls it “an order to be kind to slaves” and gives the Prophet's last counsel on the prayer and on slaves.
verse-4-36.takeaway: Ibn Kathīr on 4:36: “This is an order to be kind to slaves, because the slave is weak and helpless, held as a captive in the hands of people.”

items.text: and the companion at your side, and the traveler, and what your right (hands) own. Surely God does not love anyone who is arrogant (and) boastful,
This is an order to be kind to slaves, because the slave is weak and helpless, held as a captive in the hands of people.

items.work: in his last illness, in a report Ibn Kathīr calls authentic, on 4:36
items.text: (Protect) the prayer, (protect) the prayer, and (those slaves) what your right hands possess.

because the slaves belonging to any of us are under his hands, and they only eat what our right hands hand over, and wear what they clothe them with, and you direct them in whatever you love to direct them in with it.

tafsirQuotes.who: The Prophet, from Abū Hurayra, as Ibn Kathīr gives it (“Muslim also recorded this Hadith”)
tafsirQuotes.text: The slave has the right to have food and clothing, and is only required to perform what he can bear of work.
from what God has bestowed upon you. All of this, God has enjoined.

classical.text: Ibn Kathīr calls the phrase “an order to be kind to slaves” and supports it with reports of the Prophet: his last counsel on the prayer and on slaves, and the slave's right “to have food and clothing”. Al-Ṭabarī explains the phrase “what your right (hands) own” by daily life: “they only eat what our right hands hand over”.

verse-4-36.comparison: Both commentators read the phrase as slaves and the command as kindness to them; no premise here is in dispute. Ibn Kathīr gives the reason, the slave is “held as a captive in the hands of people”, and al-Ṭabarī explains the phrase by daily life: slaves “only eat what our right hands hand over”. The verse sets slaves at the end of the same list as parents, orphans and neighbours, and closes on a warning: “Surely God does not love anyone who is arrogant (and) boastful,” (4:36)

relatedNote.title: Related verses on freeing and captives
relatedNote.intro: Other verses Muslims cite on freeing slaves and on captives. They are not among the 16 passages above. The three verses of expiation (kaffāra) each give a fast to the one who “does not find (the means to do that)”. Each verse links to al-Ṭabarī's commentary.
